You use the future to make guesses about the present (¿dónde estará?), the future perfect for what will be done by a certain time (habremos terminado) and to guess about the past (habrá tenido una urgencia), plus the conditional for guesses about the past (serían las diez).
must be, will be (a guess about the present)
Where can Mihai be? It’s already eleven.
He must have had an emergency at the hospital.
By the summer we’ll have finished the house.
When I arrived, it must have been ten o’clock.
In a year, Rosa Elena will already have learned to walk.
To use the simple future for guesses about the PRESENT: estará en casa (he’s probably at home).
To form the future perfect: habré, habrás, habrá… + participle.
To say what will be done by a certain time: para el verano habremos terminado.
To guess what happened: habrá perdido el autobús (he must have missed the bus).
To make guesses about the past with the conditional: serían las diez (it must have been ten).
A March evening. Mihai was supposed to be home at seven. It’s eleven and he isn’t answering his phone. Ana calls Elena, who is still staying with them but has gone round to Mrs Maria’s.
(on the phone, in slow Spanish) Elena, have you heard from Mihai? It’s eleven and he hasn’t come home.
(in very simple Spanish) I don’t know… He’ll be at the hospital. Lots of work.
But he isn’t answering. I’ve called him ten times.
Calm down. He’ll have run out of battery. He always forgets to charge it.
Yes, that’s possible. Or he’ll have had an emergency. He’s on call this week.
Sure. My son is good doctor. A patient… heart problem. He works.
You’re right. He must be about to arrive. Thank you, Elena.
(half an hour later, coming in) Sorry, sorry… My battery died and there was a terrible traffic jam.
Your mother was right. She told me your battery would have died. What happened?
At six a man came in with a heart attack. I operated on him for three hours. He’s fine now.
Poor man… How old would he have been?
I don’t know. He must have been about seventy. Like my dad. That’s why I stayed a bit longer, to talk to his family.
You did the right thing. Come on, sit down. You’ll have eaten something at least, won’t you?
A coffee at five. Nothing else.
Then there are sarmale. There are always sarmale. By the time Rosa Elena turns one, we’ll have eaten a thousand.
A thousand at least. Hey, and the baby? Will she have fallen asleep by now?
Two hours ago. But I’m sure that as soon as you sit down, she’ll wake up. She has radar for that.

a-BRA (future) versus a-BREE-a (conditional). The only difference is the last syllable: -RÁ or -RÍA.
“¿Dónde estará?” is said in a thoughtful, slightly lowered voice, as if you were talking to yourself.
Elena speaks “telegraphic” Spanish: short sentences, no conjunctions. That’s normal at the start. You spoke Japanese like that too!
1. The future as a guess about the PRESENT
Surprise: in Spanish, the simple future isn’t only for the future. It’s used VERY often to guess about NOW. English does something similar: “That’ll be the postman”, “He’ll be at work by now”:
Estará en el hospital. (He’ll be at the hospital / He must be at the hospital.)
Serán las diez. (It must be about ten.)
Tendrá setenta años. (He must be about seventy.)
Questions in the future express wonder or worry: ¿Dónde estará? (Where can he be? / I wonder where he is), ¿Quién será a estas horas? (Who can that be at this hour?).
First meaning: an action that WILL BE DONE before a moment in the future. It’s often used with “para + time” or “dentro de”, just like English “by…” and “in…”:
In a year she’ll have learned to walk.
3. The future perfect as a guess about the past
Second meaning, very common in conversation: you guess what HAS HAPPENED (recent past), like English “he must have…” / “he’ll have…”:
Se habrá quedado sin batería. (He must have run out of battery.)
The logical pattern: present → simple future (estará). Pretérito perfecto → future perfect (habrá estado). Every “certain” tense has its “guess” partner.
4. The conditional as a guess about the past
To guess about the more distant past (imperfect / indefinido), use the CONDITIONAL:
Serían las diez. (It must have been ten.)
Don’t confuse it with the “polite” conditional (me gustaría) or the “hypothetical” one (si tuviera, haría). Context decides: «Cuando llegué, serían las diez» is clearly a guess.

In April, Grandpa Gheorghe did something he hadn’t done in ninety-two years: he came to Bucharest. Nobody expected it. He never left his village. He said the city was noisy, dirty and full of people always in a hurry.
But one Tuesday morning, Mihai got a phone call from his father, Ion. Grandpa had got on the six o’clock train on his own. With his old hat, his walking stick and a cloth bag.
“And why didn’t he tell us?” asked Mihai.
“Because he knew you’d tell him not to come,” his father answered. “He arrives at Gara de Nord at twelve. If you don’t pick him up, he’ll get lost.”

Mihai left the hospital at half past eleven. At five to twelve he was on the platform, anxious. The train arrived twenty minutes late. People began to get off: students, families, ladies with huge suitcases.
But Grandpa didn’t appear. Mihai walked the platform from one end to the other. Where could he be? Had he got on the wrong train? Had he fallen asleep and gone on to the next town?

Finally he saw him. He was in the last carriage, chatting calmly with the ticket inspector. They were both laughing. Grandpa had offered him a piece of cheese from his bag, and the inspector had accepted.
“Grandpa!” Mihai shouted. “The train got in ten minutes ago!”
Grandpa looked at him as if he didn’t understand the hurry. “I know,” he said. “But this gentleman has a daughter who lives in my village. I couldn’t get off without finishing the conversation.”

On the way home, Grandpa looked out of the car window with wide eyes. He hadn’t seen Bucharest for seventy years. The last time he had come as a young man, to sell sheep at a market that no longer existed.
“All this used to be fields,” he said, pointing at the tall blocks of flats. “There was a little river here where children swam in summer.”
Grandpa took a while to answer. “There are too many cars. And nobody looks at anybody. But the acacias still smell the same. Nobody has changed that.”
When they reached the house in the old neighbourhood, Grandpa stood in front of the gate for a long time. Mr Ilie had finished the roof and was painting the balcony dark green.

Grandpa had never been in that house. It was Elena’s family’s house, not his. But he had heard it talked about many times. And he knew the story of Grandpa Vasile, the soldier who came back from the war with a ring made from a coin.
“I knew him,” he said suddenly. “Vasile. We were at the front together, in forty-four. He was younger than me. He was always talking about a girl waiting for him in Bucharest. Her name was Ileana.”
Mihai froze. So did Ana, who had just come out into the yard with the baby in her arms.
“Why did you never tell us?” Mihai asked, his voice shaking.
“Because I didn’t know,” Grandpa answered. “Until your father told me about the box under the floor, I didn’t know that Vasile was my daughter-in-law’s father. There are a lot of Vasiles in Romania.”
“Is that why you came?” Ana asked, in her still clumsy Romanian.
Grandpa looked at her and smiled. “For that and for the little one. You don’t reach ninety-two to stay at home when important things are happening.”

That afternoon, Grandpa sat on the freshly painted balcony with Rosa Elena in his arms. He talked to her softly for hours. Nobody ever found out what he told her. Mihai said later it must have been war stories, or stories about sheep, or about white she-bears.
The baby didn’t cry once. She fell asleep listening to him, holding on to Grandpa’s finger.
At dusk, Mrs Maria looked over the fence. She looked at Grandpa for a while. Then she said something out loud, and Grandpa answered her. They both burst out laughing.
“What did they say?” Ana asked Mihai.
“Mrs Maria told him he was the most handsome man to walk down this street in seventy years. And Grandpa answered that, at his age, that wasn’t much of an achievement.”

Grandpa stayed three days. On the third day, before going back to the village, he gave Mihai something he kept in his coat pocket: a small black-and-white photo of two young soldiers sitting on a rock.
One of them was Grandpa Gheorghe. The other had the same face as the soldier in the photo in the box: Vasile.
“Put it in the box,” Grandpa told him. “So they’re together again. By the time the next person opens it, neither of us two will be here any more. But the photo will still be there.”
That same evening, Mihai lifted the lid in the living-room floor. He opened the wooden box very carefully and placed the photo of the two soldiers next to Grandma Ileana’s letter and the silver ring.
Ana, sitting beside him with the sleeping baby, asked softly: “Do you think they’ll have met again, wherever they are?”
Mihai closed the box and put the lid back. “I don’t know,” he answered. “But here, at least, they’re together now.”
